Benchmarking Document Parsers on
Mathematical Formula Extraction from PDFs
Pius Horn1[0009−0004−1911−1138] and Janis Keuper1,2[0000−0002−1327−1243]
1 Institute for Machine Learning and Analytics (IMLA), Oﬀenburg University,
Oﬀenburg, Germany pius.horn@hs-offenburg.de
2 University of Mannheim, Mannheim, Germany
Abstract. Correctly parsing mathematical formulas from PDFs is crit-
ical for training large language models and building scientiﬁc knowledge
bases from academic literature, yet existing benchmarks either exclude
formulas entirely or lack semantically-aware evaluation metrics. We in-
tro

Figure 1, part 3 'Evaluation Pipeline': a PDF-Parser produces Parsed Text (TXT); together with Ground Truth (JSON list of text, inline-formula and display-formula items) it feeds 'LLM-Based Matching (+ Rule-Based Post-Verification)', which outputs Formula Pairs (JSON of gt_formula/parsed_formula, e.g. $a+1$ vs $a+I$) and then 'Evaluation for all formula pairs'.

Figure 1, parts 1-2: Formula Dataset (Wikipedia → Formula Extraction → Filtering + Deduplication → wikipedia-latex-formulas-319k, with a Hugging Face emoji logo), then Benchmark Dataset: randomized building blocks (Display Formulas, Text Segments, Text + Inline Formulas Mixed) form a Ground Truth JSON, combined with a randomized Layout/Style LaTeX template into an assembled TEX file, compiled by pdflatex into the PDF to be parsed.

Two formula comparisons rendered by the CDM tool (green boxes = matched symbols, red = errors), each with a score table. Left: 778320/2598960 vs 778120/2598960 (one digit red): LLM-Judge 3, CDM 0.929, human scores 1, 3, 9. Right: (1 + r/n)^n vs (1 + r/a)^n (denominator red): LLM-Judge 2, CDM 0.875, human scores 1, 4, 7.

Four ground-truth/parsed formula pairs separated by a blue line, all symbols boxed green: 7^2 vs 72, 10^{-1} vs 10 − 1, x_{(i−1)} vs x(i − 1), and blackboard ℕ ⊂ ℝ vs italic N ⊂ R. These are the examples of CDM giving matches despite positional or symbol differences.
Four formula pairs that look equivalent but where CDM boxes the middle symbol in red: A ∧ B, A \ B = 0, x → y, and x ≠ y, each shown above and below a blue line with the operands boxed green.
